section.title: Rahab and the Spies
section.sectionRationale: Before Israel crosses the Jordan, Joshua sends two spies into Jericho, and the story turns unexpectedly on a Canaanite prostitute. Rahab hides the spies, confesses that the LORD is God of heaven and earth, and pleads for her family to be spared. A covenant is struck, sealed by a scarlet cord, and the spies return with a report not of Israel's strength but of God's terror already fallen on the land. It is one movement, the surprising conversion and rescue of an outsider on the eve of conquest.
section.thesis: On the threshold of a war of judgment, God shows that His purpose is not the destruction of every Canaanite but the salvation of all who take refuge in Him, as a pagan prostitute, hearing what God has done, believes, acts on her faith, and is drawn by grace into the covenant people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the spies enter and Rahab hides them, verses 1 to 7; Rahab's confession of the LORD, verses 8 to 11; the covenant and the scarlet cord, verses 12 to 21; and the spies' report that the land is already melting in fear, verses 22 to 24.

units.label: The spies enter and Rahab hides them
units.note: she hid them among the flax on the roof

verses.text: Then Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two spies from Shittim, saying, “Go, inspect the land, especially Jericho.” So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there.
And it was reported to the king of Jericho: “Behold, some men of Israel have come here tonight to spy out the land.”
So the king of Jericho sent to Rahab and said, “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, for they have come to spy out the whole land.”
But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. So she said, “Yes, the men did come to me, but I did not know where they had come from.
At dusk, when the gate was about to close, the men went out, and I do not know which way they went. Pursue them quickly, and you may catch them!”
(But Rahab had taken them up to the roof and hidden them among the stalks of flax that she had laid out there.)
So the king’s men set out in pursuit of the spies along the road to the fords of the Jordan, and as soon as they had gone out, the gate was shut.

units.label: Rahab's confession of the LORD
units.note: the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below

verses.text: Before the spies lay down for the night, Rahab went up on the roof
and said to them, “I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you.

For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites across the Jordan, whom you {{cherem|devoted to destruction}}.
When we heard this, our hearts melted and everyone’s courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.

units.label: The covenant and the scarlet cord
units.note: swear to me by the LORD; the scarlet cord in the window

verses.text: Now therefore, please swear to me by the LORD that you will indeed show {{chesed|kindness}} to my family, because I showed kindness to you. Give me a sure sign
that you will spare the lives of my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and that you will deliver us from death.”
“Our lives for your lives!” the men agreed. “If you do not report our mission, we will show you kindness and {{emeth|faithfulness}} when the LORD gives us the land.”
Then Rahab let them down by a rope through the window, since the house where she lived was built into the wall of the city.
“Go to the hill country,” she said, “so that your pursuers will not find you. Hide yourselves there for three days until they have returned; then go on your way.”
The men said to her, “We will not be bound by this oath you made us swear

unless, when we enter the land, you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and unless you have brought your father and mother and brothers and all your family into your house.

If anyone goes out the door of your house into the street, his blood will be on his own head, and we will be innocent. But if a hand is laid on anyone with you in the house, his blood will be on our heads.
And if you report our mission, we will be released from the oath you made us swear.”
“Let it be as you say,” she replied, and she sent them away. And when they had gone, she tied the scarlet cord in the window.

units.label: The spies report the land melting in fear
units.note: the LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands

verses.text: So the spies went out into the hill country and stayed there three days, until their pursuers had returned without finding them, having searched all along the road.
Then the two men started back, came down from the hill country, and crossed the river. So they came to Joshua son of Nun and reported all that had happened to them.
“The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands,” they said to Joshua. “Indeed, all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of us.”

cherem.gloss: That which is devoted to destruction, set apart irrevocably to the LORD, whether by destroying it or offering it. Rahab has heard how Israel devoted Sihon and Og to destruction. The word names the solemn, God-ordained judgment about to fall on Canaan; the wonder of this chapter is that a woman who names this very judgment is herself spared, drawn out from under the ban by faith.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, kindness that keeps faith. Rahab asks the spies to show her chesed because she has shown chesed to them, and they swear it. This is the great covenant word used again and again of the LORD's own loyal love; here it binds an Israelite oath to a Canaanite believer, a picture of covenant mercy reaching beyond Israel.

emeth.gloss: Truth, faithfulness, reliability. Paired with chesed, kindness and faithfulness, verse 14, it forms the well-known covenant couplet describing dependable, promise-keeping love. The spies pledge not mere goodwill but faithfulness, a sworn commitment they will keep, mirroring the steadfast love and truth of the God in whose name they swear.

basic.context: Joshua sends two spies into Jericho, and they end up in the house of Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute. When the king's men come looking, Rahab hides the spies and sends the search off in the wrong direction. Then she tells the spies why: she has heard how the LORD rescued Israel from Egypt and defeated the kings east of the Jordan, and she now believes that the LORD is God of heaven and earth. She asks that when Israel takes the city, her family will be spared. The spies swear an oath, sealed by a scarlet cord she must tie in her window. They return to Joshua reporting that the land is already terrified, because God has gone ahead of them. The question at the heart of it is: who can be saved when God's judgment comes?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and it sits inside the hard reality of the conquest, the herem, God's judgment on Canaan. The chapter is not primarily about spy craft or even about Rahab's lie, which the text neither commends as a rule nor dwells on, but about faith. Rahab is held up in the New Testament as an example of saving faith that acts, James 2:25, and as a woman justified by faith, Hebrews 11:31. We read her story as a bright thread of mercy running through a chapter about judgment.
basic.originalLanguages: Rahab names the cherem, the devotion to destruction, that fell on Sihon and Og and is coming to Canaan. Yet she asks for chesed, covenant kindness, and the spies swear chesed and emeth, kindness and faithfulness, the great couplet of God's own loyal love. The vocabulary of judgment and the vocabulary of covenant mercy meet in one Canaanite woman.
basic.typology: The scarlet cord in Rahab's window, marking the house where her family will be safe when destruction sweeps the city, recalls the blood on the doorposts at Passover and points to the blood of Christ, under which sinners are sheltered from judgment. Rahab herself, an outsider brought into Israel, foreshadows the nations gathered into God's people through faith.
basic.christ: Rahab, a Gentile and a prostitute, is saved by faith and welcomed into Israel, and she appears in the very genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5. She is a living sign that Christ came to save sinners and outsiders, and that no one is beyond His mercy. The scarlet cord that shelters her household points to the blood of Christ, the sure sign under which all who believe are spared.
basic.god: God is the sovereign Judge whose acts in Egypt and beyond the Jordan have already gone ahead of Israel, melting the courage of Canaan. He is God in heaven above and on earth below, as even a pagan woman confesses. And He is the God of mercy, who does not delight in the death of the wicked but saves the one who turns to Him, even a Canaanite prostitute on the eve of judgment.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 11 lists Rahab among the heroes of faith. James 2 points to her as faith proved by works. Matthew 1 places her in the family tree of Jesus. And Exodus 12 tells of the blood on the doorposts, the pattern the scarlet cord recalls.
basic.oneStory: As Israel stands ready to enter the land under God's judgment, God plucks one believing outsider out of a doomed city and brings her into His people. Rahab's rescue by faith, sealed with a scarlet cord, points ahead to the salvation of the nations and to the blood of Christ under which every believing sinner is sheltered.

context.literary:
Joshua 2 is built as a tight envelope: spies sent out in verse 1 and spies returned in verses 23 to 24, with the narrator's summary in verse 24 answering the commissioning in verse 1 almost word for word, so the whole chapter reads as one completed errand framed by report. Inside that envelope the scene divides sharply by speaker. The king of Jericho speaks through messengers who never appear in person, a paper authority contrasted with Rahab, who speaks for herself at every turn and controls the pace of the action: she hides, she misdirects, she negotiates, she ties the cord. Direct speech dominates the chapter, roughly two thirds of its verses are dialogue, which is unusual for Joshua's mostly summary battle reports and signals that the author wants us listening to what people say about God, not just watching what armies do.

The chapter is also a deliberate counter text to the spy story a generation earlier. Numbers 13 and 14 sent twelve spies who returned with a report of giants and fortified cities and produced unbelief that cost Israel forty years. Joshua's two spies bring back the opposite verdict, drawn not from their own courage but from a Canaanite's testimony, and their report in verse 24 is framed to answer Numbers 13:31 to 33 almost point for point. The irony that the truest theology in the chapter comes from the mouth of a pagan prostitute, while the king of Jericho commands and is ignored, sets up the whole conquest narrative: victory belongs to those who trust the LORD's word, whoever they are.
context.historical:
Jericho at this date was among the oldest fortified sites in the land, controlling the natural approach from the Jordan valley into the central hill country, which is exactly why Joshua's spies are sent there rather than anywhere else; whoever holds Jericho holds the door to Canaan. A house built into the city wall, as Rahab's is described in verse 15, was a common arrangement in walled towns of the period, where the wall's own thickness could provide rooms, and a window through the outer face could let someone down outside the wall unseen, precisely the escape route the spies use. Flax laid out to dry on a flat roof belongs to the same agricultural calendar that will matter again in chapter 3: flax harvest fell in the early spring, near barley harvest and Passover, exactly the season of the Jordan crossing that follows.

City gates in the ancient Near East were shut and guarded at nightfall, both for defense and for keeping track of who entered and left, which is why the king's men can be told with confidence that the spies must have slipped out before the gate closed, and why the gate's closing behind the pursuers, verse 7, seals Jericho off from its own countryside. Rahab's request that the spies swear by the LORD, rather than by Israel's power or by her own gods, follows the common ancient Near Eastern practice of sealing an agreement with an oath invoking a deity as witness and enforcer, the same practice behind Abraham's oaths with Abimelech, Genesis 21:22 to 24. That she asks them to swear specifically by the LORD, the God whose name she has just confessed, shows she understands exactly what kind of oath will bind these men.
context.canonical:
Rahab's confession sets a pattern that plays out across the rest of the book. In chapter 9 the Gibeonites, having heard the same reports that terrified Jericho, choose the same path as Rahab: they treat the LORD's acts as decisive and seek a covenant of peace rather than a fight, and Joshua's oath spares them just as the spies' oath spared Rahab, Joshua 9:24 to 25. Against that stands Joshua 11:20, where the text states plainly that the LORD hardened the hearts of the rest of the Canaanite kings to meet Israel in battle and be destroyed, so that mercy was refused, not withheld.

Two women in Rahab's own line make the pattern explicit. Matthew's genealogy places Rahab beside Tamar, Ruth, and Bathsheba, four women marked by scandal or foreign birth rather than pedigree, showing from the very first verses of the New Testament that grace, not lineage, builds the family of the Messiah. Ruth, the next book after Joshua and Judges canonically, gives the fullest sequel: a Moabite widow who takes refuge under the LORD's wings, Ruth 2:12, using language remarkably close to Rahab's own confession, and who marries Boaz, very plausibly Rahab's own son, Matthew 1:5. The scarlet thread of an outsider woman received by covenant kindness into Israel runs directly from Jericho's wall to Bethlehem's threshing floor to the town of David.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Before Israel fights a single battle, the author places a story that reframes what conquest means: the narrator wants readers to see that the coming war is not a contest of Israelite prowess against Canaanite armies but the working out of a judgment and mercy already decided in heaven, verse 9's the LORD has given you this land spoken in the present tense before the first arrow flies. By putting these words in a Canaanite mouth rather than an Israelite one, the author is teaching Israel something uncomfortable: the nations already know what many in Israel, a generation earlier, refused to believe. The two spies who say almost nothing themselves and simply carry Rahab's confession back to Joshua become witnesses rather than heroes, so that credit for what is about to happen belongs to God's reputation preceding Israel into the land, not to reconnaissance or bravery.

The author also wants the reader to notice who survives an act of total war: not the powerful, the king of Jericho, whose messengers command and are defied, but the one who hears, believes, and acts, preparing the reader to expect more such reversals as the conquest unfolds and forcing a definition of Israel that runs along the line of faith rather than only bloodline.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is equally careful not to prescribe the specific terms of the spies' oath as a manual for treaty making. Their promise rests on conditions bound to that night and that city, a scarlet cord, a gathered household, a shut door, and it expires the moment any term is broken, verses 17 to 20; it describes one covenant transaction, not a pattern for negotiating with combatants in general.

What is prescriptive is narrower and runs underneath the specifics: a right response to God's revealed word is to act on it immediately, at cost, before the outcome is certain, which is exactly what James commends when he calls Rahab's sheltering of the spies a work that completed her faith, James 2:25. Whether her lie itself should be imitated is a separate question from whether her faith should be; the text lets her faith stand as the model while never turning her wartime deception into a commanded ethic for later readers.

debates.question: Does the chapter approve of Rahab's lie to the king of Jericho?

views.label: Her faith is commended, not her method
views.case: Scripture praises Rahab for her faith and for receiving the spies, Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25, never singling out the lie for approval; the narrative reports it as part of the account without holding it up as a model, so we honor her faith while not treating deception as a rule to follow.

views.label: The deception is a lesser act within a life and death loyalty
views.case: Some argue that Rahab, having sided with God's people against a city under judgment, acted to protect life in a wartime setting, so that her concealment is viewed sympathetically as the outworking of a new and imperfect faith turning from her old allegiances toward the LORD.

views.label: The church fathers judged the lie itself sinful
views.case: Augustine, holding that any untruth is sinful without exception, judged Rahab's lie a fault even while treating her faith and her welcome of the spies as genuinely praiseworthy, a position that keeps admiration for her faith entirely separate from any approval of the method she used.

debates.bearing: All three views agree the point of the passage is Rahab's God given faith that acts; the text leaves her deception without commendation and directs our attention to the mercy of God that saves her.

debates.question: How can the conquest of Canaan, its herem judgment, be reconciled with God's goodness?

views.label: Just judgment on entrenched wickedness, with mercy always open
views.case: The conquest is presented in Scripture as God's righteous judgment on centuries of Canaanite evil, Genesis 15:16 and Deuteronomy 9:4 to 5, a judgment He delayed for generations; Rahab shows that the door of mercy stood open to any who would turn to the LORD, so the war was never about ethnicity but about faith and unrepentant sin.

views.label: A unique, bounded act in redemptive history
views.case: The herem was a limited, God commanded event tied to a particular land and moment, not a pattern for later warfare; it dramatizes the seriousness of sin and the holiness of God, and it points forward to the final judgment, while the church's warfare is spiritual, not by the sword, 2 Corinthians 10:3 to 5.

debates.bearing: Held honestly together, these guard both truths: God's judgment on sin is real and just, and His mercy genuinely reaches even a Canaanite prostitute who believes, which is precisely why this chapter stands where it does.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the three words the basic level already names, the chapter's Hebrew repays closer attention. When Rahab asks for a sure sign, verse 12, she uses oth, the standard word for a covenant marker, the same word used of the rainbow after the flood, Genesis 9:12 to 13, and of the blood on Egypt's doorposts, Exodus 12:13. She is not asking for a vague assurance but for the kind of concrete, visible token Scripture elsewhere attaches to God's own covenants, and the spies answer in kind with the scarlet cord.

The oath itself, please swear to me by the LORD, uses the verb shava, built on the same root as the number seven, since ancient oaths were sometimes sealed by seven witnesses or a sevenfold gesture, as when Abraham sets apart seven ewe lambs to seal his covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba, the well of the oath, Genesis 21:28 to 31. Rahab knows exactly what she is asking, a solemn, binding commitment before the God whose name she has confessed.

The couplet the spies actually promise, chesed and emeth, kindness and faithfulness, verse 14, is not a phrase invented for this scene. Chesed we'emeth, or its close relative, is a fixed pairing that runs through the Torah and the Psalms as the vocabulary of God's own covenant loyalty: it describes the LORD's dealings with Abraham's servant, Genesis 24:27, His own self revelation to Moses, Exodus 34:6, and His faithful love celebrated in the Psalms, Psalm 25:10 and Psalm 61:7. When Israelite men swear this precise covenant pair to a Canaanite woman, the narrator is quietly saying that she is being treated, in language, exactly as the LORD treats His own.

Cherem, meanwhile, is a wider word than devotion to destruction alone. Its root sense is to set something apart irrevocably, and Leviticus can use it of things given over to the sanctuary rather than destroyed, Leviticus 27:28. Rahab has heard it used only in its terrible sense, of Sihon and Og, and she names it rightly as the doom bearing down on her own city; the wonder of the chapter is that the same root that seals Jericho's fate has no power to hold a woman who has crossed, in her confession, from the side under the ban to the side bound by covenant kindness. Even her own name plays into this movement: Rahab, meaning wide or spacious, belongs to a woman whose house is built into a narrow city wall and who herself becomes, by faith, a spacious door through which an outsider's whole family walks into Israel.

typology.type: The scarlet cord marking the house to be spared in the city's destruction
typology.fulfillment: Exodus 12:13 hangs Israel's safety from the tenth plague on a sign painted where it could be seen, blood on doorposts, and the destroyer passes over every house that bears it. Rahab's scarlet cord works the same way: a visible mark on a specific house, tied in place before the danger arrives, and it must still be there when judgment falls, Joshua 2:18. Both point to the blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19, the sign under which every believing household shelters. The type falls short in that a cord or blood mark had to be renewed and reapplied for each household and each generation; the blood of Christ marks His people once, permanently, and never has to be tied again.

typology.type: Rahab the Canaanite outsider brought into Israel by faith
typology.fulfillment: Rahab crosses from a city under the ban to a place inside Israel's own family line, marrying into Judah's tribe and appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5, a status no bloodline could have earned her. Paul describes exactly this movement for every Gentile believer: once separate from Christ, excluded from Israel's covenants and without hope, but now brought near through the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:12 to 13. Rahab is a single, concrete instance of a pattern the gospel makes universal. The type is not exact, since Rahab still had to be grafted into an existing earthly nation, while the church Paul describes is a wholly new humanity, neither Jew nor Gentile but one new man in Christ, Ephesians 2:14 to 15.

typology.type: The LORD's terror going ahead to melt the land before Israel arrives
typology.fulfillment: The spies' final report, the LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands, verse 24, credits a victory not yet fought to God's prior action; the courage of Canaan failed before a single Israelite crossed the river. Paul draws the same conclusion for every battle a believer faces: if God is for us, who can be against us, Romans 8:31, and thanks be to God who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 15:57. The pattern is that faith counts on a triumph God has already secured rather than a triumph still to be won. Where it falls short as a type is that Jericho's fear was fear of judgment, while the confidence Paul describes is the settled peace of those already reconciled to the Judge Himself.

typology.type: Rahab's whole household spared through one woman's faith and oath, Joshua 2:13 and 2:18
typology.fulfillment: The covenant reaches further than Rahab alone: her father, mother, brothers, sisters, and all who belong to them are named in the promise and must simply be gathered inside her house when judgment falls, verses 13 and 18 to 19. The pattern surfaces again when Paul tells the Philippian jailer, believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household, Acts 16:31, and Peter's whole household believes with him, Acts 10:44 to 48. A household is drawn to safety through the faith of the one who first believed and acted on it. The type falls short of exact correspondence, since Scripture elsewhere makes plain that each person must personally believe; the household is gathered under one roof, but each member still crosses the threshold by their own faith, not by another's alone.

study.christ:
Jesus draws exactly this line when He tells the chief priests and elders that tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God ahead of them, Matthew 21:31 to 32, because sinners who hear and believe outrun the religious who merely hear and argue. Rahab is the Old Testament proof of His point centuries in advance: a woman with her trade named plainly, whose only qualification is that she believed what she heard about the LORD and acted on it before anyone else in her city did. When Jesus later tells a sinful woman who has anointed His feet, your faith has saved you, go in peace, Luke 7:50, the same word for peace echoes Hebrews' description of Rahab, who welcomed the spies in peace, Hebrews 11:31. Faith that hears the truth about God and moves toward Him, whatever a person's past, is met with peace rather than exclusion, in the Old Testament and in the Gospels alike.

The scarlet cord's fulfillment in Christ's blood runs further than a single image of shelter. Joshua 6:22 to 25 records that the city and everyone in it was destroyed except Rahab, her father's household, and all she had, because she hid the messengers Joshua sent; the oath sworn in chapter 2 is literally kept in chapter 6, judgment falling on every side of her house while her own household stands. That is the shape of the gospel in miniature: the same day wrath falls, mercy holds, for those marked by the sign the Judge Himself provided. Rahab does not survive judgment by escaping the city before it falls or by her own strength; she survives inside the very city under the ban, sheltered by a covenant sign she did nothing to invent.

Her place in Matthew's genealogy deserves a second look beside her Gentile status. She marries Salmon, apparently a prince of Judah's own tribe, the line already carrying the promise of Genesis 49:10 that the scepter would not depart from Judah, and their son Boaz becomes the kinsman redeemer of another outsider, Ruth the Moabite, whose son Obed becomes the grandfather of David, Matthew 1:5 to 6. Two Gentile women, spared by covenant kindness and drawn into Judah's royal line within a few generations of each other, become the great grandmothers of Israel's greatest king and, through him, ancestors of great David's greater Son. The gospel that welcomes outsiders is not a New Testament innovation grafted onto an exclusive Old Testament story; Jericho's scarlet cord and Bethlehem's kinsman redeemer both belong to the same design, centuries before the cross makes the design plain.
study.god:
This chapter also shows a God who works by ordinary means without ceasing to be sovereign. He does not need spies to learn Jericho's condition; He uses them anyway, sending two ordinary men on a risky errand so that Israel would receive, in a Canaanite woman's own words, confirmation of what He had already decided. The pattern recurs throughout the conquest: God's decree and human action are never rivals in this book, human obedience is simply how His decree reaches the people who need to hear it.

His patience stands behind the very moment this story occurs. Centuries earlier God had told Abraham that his descendants would not possess the land immediately, because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet complete, Genesis 15:16. Jericho's destruction is not an impulsive act of a tribal war god; it is judgment delayed for generations, falling only when the LORD determines that patience has run its full course. That same patience is what makes room for one household inside the doomed city to be spared: judgment on a nation and mercy on a person coexist because both rest in the same unhurried, righteous decision of the same God.

The chapter also reveals a God who lets Himself be known outside His covenant people before He is known by them formally. Rahab's theology, that the LORD is God in the heavens above and on the earth below, verse 11, is exact and correct, and she reaches it from reports carried by rumor into a hostile city, not from priestly instruction or a direct encounter. It is a striking claim about how God makes Himself known: His mighty acts, retold even by frightened enemies, are enough to produce real faith in a heart ready to respond, though that faith still needs the spies' word and oath to be completed in covenant belonging. And He is a God whose justice and mercy are never divided into separate compartments applied to separate people; the same acts at the Red Sea and against Sihon and Og that doom Jericho to fear are the acts that convince Rahab to believe, so that one report produces both the city's collapse and one woman's rescue, depending entirely on what the hearer does with it.

crossReferences.note: Rahab is named among heroes whose faith is proven by action, tied to the phrase that she did not perish with the disobedient, a phrase that assumes the reader already knows exactly who did perish, the rest of Jericho.
James picks the same episode to prove that a claimed faith which produces no action is dead; Rahab's hiding and misdirecting the king's men is offered as the working proof of a faith already present.

Rahab is named as the mother of Boaz within a few generations of Jesus' own genealogy, placing a Canaanite prostitute inside the family line the Gospel opens with, before a single miracle is recorded.

The blood marking Israelite doorposts causes the destroyer to pass over; Rahab's scarlet cord marks a single house inside a doomed city in exactly the same way, a sign that must be visibly in place when judgment comes.
God tells Abraham centuries earlier that the conquest must wait until the iniquity of the Amorites is complete, showing Jericho's fall is patient judgment long delayed, not an impulsive act.
Abraham and Abimelech seal a peace with an oath sworn by God as witness, the same practice behind Rahab's demand that the spies swear to her by the LORD rather than merely give their word.

The oath sworn in chapter two is kept to the letter: Jericho and everyone in it is destroyed, but Rahab, her father's family, and all she has are brought out and spared, and her family lives on among Israel.

Jesus tells the religious leaders that tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom of God ahead of them, because they believed the message when it came; Rahab is the pattern centuries before He speaks the words.

Paul tells the Philippian jailer that belief in the Lord Jesus brings salvation to him and his household, the same shape as the spies' oath that Rahab's whole family would be spared through her faith.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12:3 promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's line, and Joshua 2 is the first place in the conquest narrative where that promise visibly reaches someone outside Israel by name. The book of Joshua is largely the story of judgment falling on the nations who filled the measure of their sin, Genesis 15:16, yet from the very first city, before the war has properly begun, God shows that the line separating the saved from the lost in Canaan was never the line of ethnicity; it was always the line of faith. Rahab crosses that line while an entire city refuses to, and an entire people's fear, described three times over in this short chapter, produces nothing in them but dread, while the same reports produce in her belief and action.

The prophets later promise that this will not remain a single exception. Isaiah pictures foreigners who join themselves to the LORD being brought to His holy mountain and given a name better than sons and daughters, Isaiah 56:6 to 7, and pictures the nations streaming to Zion to learn the LORD's ways, Isaiah 2:2 to 3. Rahab is the down payment on both promises, a foreigner joined to the LORD centuries before the prophets speak, brought not merely near but into the messianic line itself. The stream that begins with one woman confessing faith in a doomed city becomes, in Revelation's vision, a multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, standing before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 7:9, wearing robes made white by the very blood the scarlet cord foreshadowed.

Joshua 2 therefore sits at a hinge in the whole Bible's story of the nations: it looks back to the promise given to Abraham that blessing would reach beyond his own household, and it looks forward past the conquest, past the exile, past the New Testament's opening genealogy, to the day when every nation Israel was sent to judge in this book will instead be represented among the redeemed, saved, like Rahab, by nothing but grace received through faith in the God whose hand is mighty.

quiz.q: What did Rahab confess about the LORD to the spies?

options.text: That the LORD had given Israel the land and is God in heaven above and on earth below.
options.note: Verses 9 to 11 record her remarkable confession of faith in the true God.

options.text: That the God of Israel was one powerful god among the gods of the nations.
options.note: She goes further than this, confessing the LORD as God of heaven and earth, not merely a strong tribal deity.

options.text: That she hoped Israel's God might protect her city.
options.note: She knew the city was doomed; her plea was to be saved out of it, not that God would spare Jericho.

options.text: That she did not really believe but only wanted a bargain.
options.note: Scripture treats her words as genuine saving faith, Hebrews 11:31.

quiz.q: Why had the people of Jericho lost their courage?

options.text: They had heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea and defeated Sihon and Og, and the fear of Him had fallen on them.
options.note: Verses 9 to 11 show God's past acts had already melted the land in fear.

options.text: They had seen how large and well-armed Israel's army was.
options.note: Their fear was of what the LORD had done, not of Israel's military size; the text credits God's acts.

options.text: Their king had died and left them leaderless.
options.note: The king is still active in the chapter; their dread came from reports of the LORD's power.

options.text: A famine had weakened the city.
options.note: No famine is mentioned; their courage failed because of what they heard the LORD had done.

quiz.q: What was the sign that would spare Rahab's household?

options.text: A scarlet cord tied in her window, with her family gathered inside the house.
options.note: Verses 18 to 21 make the scarlet cord and gathering the family the condition of rescue.

options.text: A mark painted on the city gate.
options.note: The sign was a scarlet cord in her own window, not a mark on the city gate.

options.text: A password the spies gave her to shout during the battle.
options.note: There was no password; the sign was the visible scarlet cord in the window.

options.text: Nothing; the spies simply promised to remember her.
options.note: A concrete sign was required, the scarlet cord, along with keeping her family inside.

quiz.q: How does Rahab's rescue point forward in the Bible's story?

options.text: An outsider saved by faith, sheltered under a scarlet cord, foreshadowing the nations brought in and sinners sheltered by the blood of Christ.
options.note: Rahab enters Israel and the line of Jesus; the cord recalls the Passover blood, Matthew 1:5 and 1 Peter 1:19.

options.text: It shows that only ethnic Israelites could belong to God's people.
options.note: The opposite: a Canaanite is welcomed in, showing salvation reaches beyond Israel.

options.text: It teaches that God's judgment is never real, only a threat.
options.note: The judgment on Jericho was real; Rahab was genuinely rescued out from under it by faith.

options.text: It has no connection to the wider story of Scripture.
options.note: Rahab stands in the genealogy of Jesus and among the heroes of faith; her story is deeply connected.

quiz.q: What was the spies' report to Joshua?

options.text: The LORD had surely given the whole land into their hands, for its people were melting in fear.
options.note: Verse 24 records their faith-filled report, crediting the LORD for the coming victory.

options.text: The cities were too strong and the people too many to conquer.
options.note: That was the faithless report of the earlier spies in Numbers 13; these spies report confident faith.

options.text: Only Jericho could be taken, and no more.
options.note: They reported the entire land delivered into Israel's hands, not just Jericho.

options.text: Israel should turn back and settle east of the Jordan.
options.note: They urged advance, confident the LORD had given the land, not retreat.

questions: Rahab acted on the little she had heard about the LORD, while many in Israel with far more knowledge doubted. How are you responding to what God has already made known to you?
A Canaanite prostitute was welcomed into God's people and even into the line of Jesus. How does Rahab's story enlarge your sense of who God is willing to save, including yourself?
The scarlet cord marked the one safe place when judgment fell. Where are you tempted to find safety apart from the shelter God provides in Christ?
God's mighty acts had gone ahead of Israel, deciding the victory before the battle. Where do you need to trust that God has already gone before you into a situation you are facing?
Rahab risked everything to align herself with God's people against her own doomed city. Is there an old allegiance you need to leave behind to belong wholly to the LORD?

translationNotes.note: Shittim, where the spies are sent from, is also rendered Acacia Grove, as the BSB footnote notes; it was Israel's camp on the plains of Moab.
Devoted to destruction renders a form of the Hebrew cherem; the BSB footnote explains it as giving persons or things over to the LORD, by destroying or offering them.
The Red Sea is also rendered the Sea of Reeds, as the BSB footnote notes; it recalls the great deliverance of the exodus, Exodus 14.
